title: C# binding: a tree-owned Node's native object is disposed under its live C# wrapper on linux-arm64 headless servers — delayed SIGSEGV (si_addr 0x10) ~20–60 min into container runs, dumps available
body:
# Bug report — Godot issue template shape

## Tested versions

- Reproducible in: **4.7.2.stable.mono.official** (all six observed deaths across six separate boots; this is the only engine version the workload has run on).

## System information

- **Linux arm64** (Ubuntu 24.04 container image, `dotnet/runtime:10.0` base) inside Apple `container` CLI VMs on an **Apple Silicon** host (macOS), headless dedicated server, 4 vCPU / 3 GB cgroup limit.
- **Not reproducible** in the same build on **macOS native** (same machine, same silicon, same workload — many hours of soak, zero crashes) and so far **not reproduced** on x86_64 Linux under Proxmox LXC (a build has been running there as a deliberate contrast; previously a prior build ran 5 days continuous on it).

## Issue description

On a headless dedicated server, a tree-owned `Node` (the host's standing player node, parented under the scene) has its **native object disposed while its C# wrapper stays alive and referenced** — the wrapper is still held by a `GetNodesInGroup` snapshot and a registry. The next managed→native call on that wrapper (reading `GlobalPosition`) dereferences the dead native pointer and the process dies with **SIGSEGV at `si_addr = 0x10` (`SEGV_MAPERR`)** — a null-pointer + field-offset read, i.e. a disposed-object access, not heap corruption (two independent full-heap dumps, identical crash site both times, kernel signal notes verified).

Onset is random, ~20–60 minutes after boot — 6 crashes in 6 container boots, always the main thread, always after the workload has been ticking idle (no clients connected at death time in the cleanest case). After the crash, a `createdump` full-heap artifact confirms: no managed exception, the managed stack is short and clean (`_PhysicsProcess → enemy tick → movement-noise emission → player-group iteration`), and the heap contains exactly the expected live objects.

We audited our own code: **no managed disposal path touches these nodes** — they are only ever `QueueFree`d (deferred, tree-owned) and the container deaths happen with zero clients connected, so no peer-driven removal runs at all. The disposal itself is the mystery: something on the native/binding side retires a tree-owned node's object ~20–60 minutes in.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Export a `.NET` ARM64 Linux build of a Godot project whose headless server scene keeps a tree-owned `Node2D` registered in a node group, with a per-physics-frame workload that iterates that group and reads `GlobalPosition` on each member (any ambient simulation touching the group every frame).
2. Run it inside an ARM64 Linux container (4 vCPU, ~3 GB) with no clients connected.
3. Wait 20–60 minutes.
4. The process dies with SIGSEGV on the main thread; `createdump` shows `Crashing thread 0001 signal 11`.

Observed 6 times in 6 boots across two container instances. The same binary and workload on macOS native has never crashed.

## Minimal reproduction project (MRP)

N/A — not yet extracted. The trigger is a workload- and timing-dependent native disposal inside a full dedicated-server scene (thousands of live nodes, networking, world residency); no minimal reproduction has been isolated yet. The complete server build, the persistent world, and **two full-heap `createdump` dumps** (ARM64 Linux, .NET 10) are available privately on request.

## Notes / questions for the bugsquad

1. Is there a known binding-lifetime issue where a tree-owned node's native object is disposed while its C# wrapper remains referenced (GC-finalizer interaction, refcount underflow in the .NET hosting layer)?
2. Should managed→native calls on wrappers whose native handle is dead be hardened in the binding (managed-side `IsInstanceValid`-style guard or an explicit raised error instead of a process-fatal SIGSEGV)?
3. We can produce additional dumps, run instrumented builds, or test candidate fixes — the reproduction is on-demand (every container boot dies within ~an hour).


---
**Cross-reference:** the same crash is also filed against dotnet/runtime ([dotnet/runtime#135693](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/135693)) — the crash surfaces in the .NET-hosted binding path, so the disposal may live on either side of the hosting boundary. Two full-heap `createdump` dumps are available privately on request.
